examples: The lake was glassy at dawn.
The water got glassier as the wind died down.

senses.head: Of eyes: fixed and showing no feeling
examples: He stared at me with glassy eyes.
Her eyes went glassy with fever.

entries.contrast: a glass door uses the noun glass; glassy never means 'made of glass', only 'like glass'.

entries.meaning: Glazed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He ate two glazed donuts on the way in.
The ham is glazed with brown sugar.
By the third hour their eyes were glazed.
He had a glazed look and hadn't heard a word.

senses.head: Covered with a shiny coating, especially food
examples: He ate two glazed donuts on the way in.
The ham is glazed with brown sugar.

senses.head: Of eyes: dull and showing no interest
examples: By the third hour their eyes were glazed.
He had a glazed look and hadn't heard a word.

entries.contrast: For eyes, the usual phrase is glazed over: My eyes glazed over halfway through.

entries.meaning: Shining brightly, usually because it is clean or new. ---
examples: The kitchen was gleaming after she scrubbed it.
A gleaming new truck sat in the driveway.
His shoes were gleaming.

entries.meaning: Openly delighted, sometimes at another's expense. ---
examples: The kids were gleeful when school was canceled.
He wore a gleeful grin all afternoon.
The commentators were gleeful about the upset.
entries.contrast: Often carries a hint of enjoying somebody else's trouble.

entries.meaning: Spoken easily and smoothly, but without real thought or honesty. ---
examples: He gave a glib answer and moved on.
That's a glib explanation for a complicated problem.
The more he talked, the glibber he sounded.
entries.contrast: Always a criticism: smooth talk that comes too easily to be sincere.

entries.meaning: Shining faintly and unsteadily. ---
examples: Glimmering lights lined the harbor.
A glimmering strip of water showed between the trees.
The candles were still glimmering at midnight.

entries.meaning: Giving off small quick flashes of reflected light. ---
examples: Sunlight caught the glinting metal of the roof.
I saw something glinting in the grass.
Her glinting eyes gave the joke away.

entries.meaning: Shining because it is wet or oily. ---
examples: His forehead was glistening with sweat.
Glistening snow covered the field.
The seals lay on the glistening rocks.
entries.contrast: glistening is the shine of something wet; gleaming is the shine of something clean or polished.

entries.meaning: Of software or equipment: full of small faults that make it work badly. ---
examples: The app is glitchy on older phones.
The video feed got glitchier as more people joined.
It's a glitchy build, but it works well enough to demo.

entries.meaning: Glittering has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore a glittering diamond necklace.
From the plane we could see the glittering lights of Las Vegas.
He left a glittering career on Wall Street to teach high school.
It was one of the most glittering parties of the year.

senses.head: Shining with many small flashes of light
examples: She wore a glittering diamond necklace.
From the plane we could see the glittering lights of Las Vegas.

senses.head: Very successful, rich or impressive
examples: He left a glittering career on Wall Street to teach high school.
It was one of the most glittering parties of the year.

entries.position: both — the 'successful' sense mostly before a noun

entries.meaning: Covered with glitter or shining like it. ---
examples: My daughter wanted glittery shoes for her birthday.
The card was so glittery that it left sparkles all over the table.
She picked the most glittery dress in the store.

entries.meaning: Global has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Global warming is changing weather patterns everywhere.
The company has a global network of suppliers.
The pandemic was truly global.
We need a global view of the budget before we cut anything.
Change the setting once and it becomes the global default.

senses.head: Affecting or including the whole world
examples: Global warming is changing weather patterns everywhere.
The company has a global network of suppliers.
The pandemic was truly global.

senses.head: Covering all parts of something; overall
examples: We need a global view of the budget before we cut anything.
Change the setting once and it becomes the global default.

entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian глобальный often just means 'huge' or 'large-scale' (глобальная проблема). English global means 'affecting the whole world' or 'overall' — for 'huge', say major, massive or large-scale.

entries.meaning: Gloomy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a cold, gloomy afternoon in November.
The basement was even gloomier than I remembered.
Why are you looking so gloomy?
Economists are gloomy about next year.
That was the gloomiest speech I've ever heard.

senses.head: Dark and gray, without much light
examples: It was a cold, gloomy afternoon in November.
The basement was even gloomier than I remembered.

senses.head: Sad and without hope
examples: Why are you looking so gloomy?
Economists are gloomy about next year.
That was the gloomiest speech I've ever heard.

entries.meaning: Made to seem more important or better than it really is. ---
examples: My title is 'manager,' but I'm really a glorified secretary.
The 'resort' was a glorified motel with a pool.
That new phone is just a glorified camera.
entries.contrast: A trap for Russian speakers: a glorified babysitter is not прославленная няня — it means the job is really just babysitting, with a grander name. The meaning is always disapproving.

entries.meaning: Glorious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The team's glorious history includes six championships.
It was a glorious victory for the small town.
We had glorious weather all week.
The view from the top was glorious.
It was the most glorious sunset I've ever seen.

senses.head: Deserving great honor and admiration
examples: The team's glorious history includes six championships.
It was a glorious victory for the small town.

senses.head: Very beautiful or enjoyable
examples: We had glorious weather all week.
The view from the top was glorious.
It was the most glorious sunset I've ever seen.

entries.meaning: Glossy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The horse had a glossy black coat.
Do you want the prints glossy or matte?
Her hair looked glossier after the treatment.
The campaign sent out a glossy brochure.
She works for a glossy fashion magazine in New York.

senses.head: Smooth and shiny
examples: The horse had a glossy black coat.
Do you want the prints glossy or matte?
Her hair looked glossier after the treatment.

senses.head: Of magazines and ads: printed on shiny paper and made to look attractive and expensive
examples: The campaign sent out a glossy brochure.
She works for a glossy fashion magazine in New York.

entries.meaning: Glowing has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We sat around the glowing coals of the campfire.
The clock's hands are glowing in the dark.
The restaurant got a glowing review in the Times.
Her boss wrote her a glowing recommendation.
I've never read a more glowing report card.
She came back from vacation tan and glowing.
His face was glowing with pride.

senses.head: Giving off a steady light or heat without flames
examples: We sat around the glowing coals of the campfire.
The clock's hands are glowing in the dark.

senses.head: Full of praise
examples: The restaurant got a glowing review in the Times.
Her boss wrote her a glowing recommendation.
I've never read a more glowing report card.

senses.head: Looking healthy, happy or excited
examples: She came back from vacation tan and glowing.
His face was glowing with pride.

entries.position: both — the 'praise' sense mostly before a noun

entries.meaning: Watching or paying attention to something so closely that you cannot stop. ---
examples: The kids were glued to the TV all morning.
She's been glued to her phone since dinner.
Everyone stayed glued to their seats until the last minute.
entries.русский: прилипший, прикованный (к экрану и т. п.)
entries.contrast: The pieces were glued together is the passive of the verb glue. The adjective is the informal 'can't look away' use: glued to the TV.

entries.meaning: Sad and quiet, often because things have gone wrong. ---
examples: The players looked glum after the loss.
Why the glum face?
He got glummer as the evening went on.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — glummer, glummest; more glum

entries.meaning: Containing no gluten, the protein in wheat, barley and rye. ---
examples: Do you have any gluten-free pasta?
The whole bakery menu is gluten-free.
She's been eating gluten-free since her diagnosis.
entries.contrast: -free means without, not at no cost: sugar-free, smoke-free, tax-free. It keeps its hyphen before a noun (gluten-free bread); after a verb many style guides keep it too.

entries.meaning: Eating, or wanting, far too much. ---
examples: After a gluttonous Thanksgiving dinner, we all fell asleep on the couch.
I felt a little gluttonous ordering a second dessert.
The company's gluttonous appetite for data worries privacy groups.

entries.meaning: Twisted, rough and full of knots, usually because of age. ---
examples: A gnarled old oak stood in the middle of the field.
My grandfather's hands were gnarled from years of farm work.
The olive trees get more gnarled every year.
entries.form: -ed from gnarl, a hard knot in wood

entries.meaning: Gnarly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He carved a walking stick from a gnarly branch.
The gnarly roots had pushed up the sidewalk.
That was a gnarly wave — I almost went under.
He has a gnarly scar on his knee from the crash.
The trail got gnarlier after the rain.

senses.head: Twisted and full of knots
examples: He carved a walking stick from a gnarly branch.
The gnarly roots had pushed up the sidewalk.

senses.head: Slang: difficult, dangerous or disgusting
examples: That was a gnarly wave — I almost went under.
He has a gnarly scar on his knee from the crash.
The trail got gnarlier after the rain.

entries.form: -y from gnarl, a hard knot in wood
entries.contrast: In American slang gnarly started with surfers and can mean 'dangerous,' 'gross' or even 'awesome' — the tone tells you which.

entries.meaning: Very bad or unpleasant. ---
examples: What's that god-awful smell?
We had to get up at some god-awful hour to catch the flight.
The coffee at that place is god-awful.
entries.comparison: not gradable — an extreme word, like terrible
entries.contrast: Informal, and some religious people find it offensive. Also written godawful.

entries.meaning: Religious and trying to live a good, moral life. ---
examples: They were hardworking, god-fearing people.
She raised her children in a god-fearing home.
My grandparents were more god-fearing than my parents.

entries.meaning: Used to show anger or annoyance, or just to add force. ---
examples: Turn off that goddamn alarm!
I can't find my goddamn keys.
It's a goddamn shame what happened to them.
entries.contrast: Rude, and offensive to many religious people. Also spelled goddam and goddamned. Before another adjective it is an adverb: It's goddamn cold.

entries.meaning: Far from everything, empty and unpleasant. ---
examples: Why would anyone build a house in this godforsaken desert?
The bus left us in some godforsaken town at two in the morning.
It was the most godforsaken place I've ever worked.

entries.meaning: Not believing in God, or not following religious rules — usually said disapprovingly. ---
examples: The preacher warned against a godless society.
Some of his neighbors thought the family was godless.
Critics called the new movie godless and violent.

entries.meaning: Like a god in power, beauty or skill. ---
examples: Fans treated the quarterback as a godlike figure.
In the old myths, the heroes had almost godlike strength.
To a five-year-old, a teenager can seem godlike.

entries.meaning: Religious and living a moral life. ---
examples: She was a kind and godly woman.
The pastor urged us to lead godly lives.
He thought he was godlier than everyone else in town.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — godlier, godliest; more godly
entries.contrast: An -ly adjective, not an adverb: a godly man, never He lived godly. Ungodly is common in at an ungodly hour ('very early').

entries.meaning: Going has 3 distinct senses.
examples: What's the going rate for a babysitter these days?
He paid well below the going price for the car.
They sold the bakery as a going concern.
Within two years the startup was a going concern.
This is the best pizza going in Chicago.
Are there any jobs going at your company?

senses.head: Usual or current at the moment — used in the going rate and the going price
examples: What's the going rate for a babysitter these days?
He paid well below the going price for the car.

senses.head: Of a business: working and making money — in a going concern
examples: They sold the bakery as a going concern.
Within two years the startup was a going concern.

senses.head: Informal, after a noun: available or existing
examples: This is the best pizza going in Chicago.
Are there any jobs going at your company?

entries.position: attributive only — but after a noun it means 'available': the best deal going

entries.meaning: Having the deep yellow color of gold. ---
examples: The trees turn red and gold in October.
The walls of the lobby were painted gold.
The logo is gold on a black background.
entries.contrast: A gold ring is made of gold — that is the noun used before another noun. As an adjective gold names the color; golden is the more literary word for it (golden hair).

entries.meaning: Of a warm brown color with yellow in it, especially food that is well cooked. ---
examples: The pie had a golden-brown crust.
Fry the onions until they are golden brown.
She had long golden-brown hair.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (a golden-brown crust), but usually two words after a verb: Bake until golden brown.

entries.meaning: Gone has 3 distinct senses.
examples: By the time I got to the station, the train was gone.
How long will you be gone?
The cookies are all gone.
The old diner on Main Street is gone now.
Their father has been gone five years now.
It's hard to believe she's really gone.

senses.head: No longer here; having left
examples: By the time I got to the station, the train was gone.
How long will you be gone?

senses.head: Used up, or no longer existing
examples: The cookies are all gone.
The old diner on Main Street is gone now.

senses.head: Dead — a gentle way to say it
examples: Their father has been gone five years now.
It's hard to believe she's really gone.

entries.contrast: She is gone describes a state — she is not here now. She has gone to work is the present perfect of the verb go.

entries.meaning: Lazy and useless. ---
examples: Her good-for-nothing brother never paid her back.
Get off the couch, you good-for-nothing bum!
The landlord called his tenants good-for-nothing freeloaders.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: He's a good-for-nothing.

entries.meaning: Kind and wanting to help other people. ---
examples: He's a good-hearted guy who would do anything for you.
The neighbors were poor but good-hearted.
She's the most good-hearted person I know.

entries.meaning: Friendly and cheerful, and not easily annoyed. ---
examples: The crowd was noisy but good-humored.
He took all the teasing in a good-humored way.
She was more good-humored about the delay than I was.
entries.contrast: American spelling humored; British good-humoured.

entries.meaning: Kind, friendly and patient; not meant to hurt. ---
examples: Our dog is big but very good-natured.
It was just some good-natured joking between friends.
He's the most good-natured kid in the class.

entries.meaning: Too eager to follow the rules and please people in charge. ---
examples: I was the goody-goody kid who always did her homework.
His goody-goody act fooled the teachers but not us.
She's a lot less goody-goody than she seems.
entries.contrast: Disapproving, and more often a noun: Don't be such a goody-goody.

entries.meaning: Soft and sticky. ---
examples: The brownies are still gooey in the middle.
The kids' hands were covered in gooey marshmallow.
These are the gooiest cinnamon rolls in town.

entries.meaning: Silly in a funny, harmless way. ---
examples: He has a goofy smile that makes everyone laugh.
Stop being goofy and eat your dinner.
That was the goofiest costume at the party.

entries.meaning: Full of blood and violence. ---
examples: The movie was too gory for the kids.
He described the accident in gory detail.
This is the goriest horror film I've ever seen.
entries.contrast: the gory details is also used as a joke about any private story: Tell me all the gory details of your date.

entries.meaning: Liking to talk about other people's private lives, or full of that kind of talk. ---
examples: Our gossipy neighbor knows everything about everyone.
The book is a gossipy account of old Hollywood.
The office got more gossipy after the layoffs.

entries.meaning: Gothic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They toured a Gothic cathedral in Cologne.
Gothic windows let in tall shafts of light.
She writes Southern Gothic novels.
The movie has a Gothic feel from the first scene.

senses.head: Of the medieval European style of building with pointed arches and tall windows
examples: They toured a Gothic cathedral in Cologne.
Gothic windows let in tall shafts of light.

senses.head: Of a dark, frightening kind of story or mood
examples: She writes Southern Gothic novels.
The movie has a Gothic feel from the first scene.

entries.meaning: Having the power to control or run an organization or country. ---
examples: The NCAA is the governing body for college sports.
The governing party lost its majority in the election.
Safety is the governing principle behind every decision we make.

entries.meaning: Relating to a government. ---
examples: The report was written by a governmental agency.
They get no governmental funding at all.
The project needs approval at several governmental levels.

entries.meaning: Graceful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dancers were incredibly graceful.
The bridge has long, graceful curves.
Cats are more graceful than dogs.
The senator gave a graceful speech after losing the race.
She found a graceful way to say no.

senses.head: Moving in a smooth, attractive way, or having a pleasing shape
examples: The dancers were incredibly graceful.
The bridge has long, graceful curves.
Cats are more graceful than dogs.

senses.head: Polite and calm in a hard situation
examples: The senator gave a graceful speech after losing the race.
She found a graceful way to say no.

entries.contrast: Russian грациозный is graceful, not gracious. Gracious is about kind, polite behavior.

entries.meaning: Gracious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Thank you for being such a gracious host.
She was gracious in defeat and congratulated the winner.
He was more gracious than I expected.
The hotel is famous for its gracious Southern style.
They live in a gracious old house near the park.

senses.head: Kind, polite and generous, especially to guests or to people with less power
examples: Thank you for being such a gracious host.
She was gracious in defeat and congratulated the winner.
He was more gracious than I expected.

senses.head: Comfortable and elegant, as enjoyed by rich people
examples: The hotel is famous for its gracious Southern style.
They live in a gracious old house near the park.

entries.contrast: A false friend: gracious is not грациозный — that is graceful. Gracious describes kind, polite behavior. Good gracious! is an old-fashioned exclamation.

entries.meaning: Gradual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There has been a gradual improvement in her health.
The change was so gradual that nobody noticed it.
Doctors recommend a more gradual return to exercise.
The trail has a gradual climb for the first mile.
The ramp is gradual enough for wheelchairs.

senses.head: Happening slowly, a little at a time
examples: There has been a gradual improvement in her health.
The change was so gradual that nobody noticed it.
Doctors recommend a more gradual return to exercise.

senses.head: Of a slope: not steep
examples: The trail has a gradual climb for the first mile.
The ramp is gradual enough for wheelchairs.

entries.meaning: Relating to university study done after a first (bachelor's) degree. ---
examples: She's a graduate student in chemistry at Berkeley.
He applied to three graduate programs.
The university offers graduate courses at night.
entries.contrast: In the US graduate school is study after a bachelor's degree — магистратура or аспирантура, not school for graduates of high school. The adjective is pronounced GRAJ-oo-uht; the verb graduate is GRAJ-oo-ayt. Don't confuse it with graduated, which describes something marked in steps (a graduated scale).

entries.meaning: Grainy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The only evidence is a grainy security video.
The photos got grainier as it got dark.
The sauce turned grainy when I heated it too fast.
This bread has a nice grainy texture.

senses.head: Of a photo or video: not clear, with many small spots
examples: The only evidence is a grainy security video.
The photos got grainier as it got dark.

senses.head: Having a rough texture with small hard pieces
examples: The sauce turned grainy when I heated it too fast.
This bread has a nice grainy texture.

entries.meaning: Grammatical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The essay had a few grammatical errors.
We studied the grammatical structure of the sentence.
Is this sentence grammatical?
It's grammatical, but no native speaker would say it.

senses.head: Relating to grammar
examples: The essay had a few grammatical errors.
We studied the grammatical structure of the sentence.

senses.head: Following the rules of grammar
examples: Is this sentence grammatical?
It's grammatical, but no native speaker would say it.

entries.position: both — sense 1 only before a noun

entries.meaning: Grand has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The hotel has a grand staircase in the lobby.
Their new house is even grander than the old one.
It was the grandest wedding the town had ever seen.
He had grand plans to travel the world.
The city is thinking about growth on a grand scale.
That comes to a grand total of $312.
She won the grand prize in the state science fair.

senses.head: Large, beautiful and impressive
examples: The hotel has a grand staircase in the lobby.
Their new house is even grander than the old one.
It was the grandest wedding the town had ever seen.

senses.head: Very ambitious; planned on a large scale
examples: He had grand plans to travel the world.
The city is thinking about growth on a grand scale.

senses.head: Total or most important — in fixed phrases like grand total and grand prize
examples: That comes to a grand total of $312.
She won the grand prize in the state science fair.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
entries.contrast: Grand is also informal for a thousand dollars — that's a noun: It cost five grand.

entries.meaning: Too big, showy or ambitious, often in a way that seems silly or unrealistic. ---
examples: The mayor announced another grandiose plan that nobody could pay for.
His ideas about himself are a little grandiose.
Each building was more grandiose than the last.
entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian грандиозный is usually praise (grand, magnificent, huge). English grandiose is disapproving — too big, too showy, or too ambitious to be realistic.

entries.meaning: Granular has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Spread the granular fertilizer evenly over the lawn.
The soil here is dry and granular.
We need more granular data to see what's going on.
The app gives you granular control over your privacy settings.

senses.head: Made of small grains or pieces
examples: Spread the granular fertilizer evenly over the lawn.
The soil here is dry and granular.

senses.head: Very detailed; broken into small parts
examples: We need more granular data to see what's going on.
The app gives you granular control over your privacy settings.

entries.meaning: In the form of small grains — especially ordinary white sugar. ---
examples: Add one cup of granulated sugar and stir.
You can use granulated garlic instead of fresh.
Make sure the coffee is finely granulated before brewing.

entries.meaning: Graphic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The show contains graphic violence.
She gave a graphic description of the attack.
The book is even more graphic than the movie.
He works as a graphic designer.
The museum has a large collection of graphic art.

senses.head: Showing or describing something, especially violence or sex, in very clear and shocking detail
examples: The show contains graphic violence.
She gave a graphic description of the attack.
The book is even more graphic than the movie.

senses.head: Relating to drawing, design or pictures
examples: He works as a graphic designer.
The museum has a large collection of graphic art.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only before a noun
entries.contrast: Graphic about violence or sex means shockingly detailed. Graphical is only about charts and computer displays (a graphical user interface).

entries.meaning: Using or relating to pictures, charts or images, especially on a computer screen. ---
examples: Windows uses a graphical user interface.
The results are shown in graphical form.
The software turns raw numbers into a graphical report.

entries.meaning: Always trying to get more money or power for yourself. ---
examples: His grasping relatives showed up as soon as he won the lottery.
The landlord was cold and grasping.
She was the most grasping politician in the state.

entries.meaning: Started or run by ordinary people rather than by leaders or big organizations. ---
examples: The park was saved by a grassroots campaign.
She began her career as a grassroots organizer in Detroit.
Their fundraising is mostly grassroots.
entries.contrast: The noun is usually two words: support from the grass roots.

entries.meaning: Covered with grass. ---
examples: We had a picnic on a grassy hill.
The backyard is grassy and flat.
Park on the grassiest part of the lot.

entries.meaning: Pleased and satisfied, especially because of something you did. ---
examples: We were gratified by the response from the community.
She was gratified to see her students succeed.
I was gratified that so many people came.
entries.takes: by or at + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: gratified is the person who is pleased; gratifying is what pleases: I was gratified by the results — The results were gratifying.

entries.meaning: Giving a feeling of satisfaction and pleasure. ---
examples: Teaching is hard but very gratifying work.
It's gratifying to see the garden finally bloom.
Winning this award is the most gratifying moment of my career.
entries.takes: to-infinitive, after it: It's gratifying to see
entries.contrast: gratifying is what pleases you; gratified is how you feel: The work is gratifying — I feel gratified.

entries.meaning: Grating has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The door made a grating noise every time it opened.
Her laugh is loud and a little grating.
His constant bragging gets grating after an hour.
The most grating thing about the ad is that song.

senses.head: Of a sound: harsh and unpleasant
examples: The door made a grating noise every time it opened.
Her laugh is loud and a little grating.

senses.head: Annoying, especially after a while
examples: His constant bragging gets grating after an hour.
The most grating thing about the ad is that song.

entries.form: -ing from grate ('to rub with a harsh noise')
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a grating is a metal frame of bars over a hole or window.

entries.meaning: Given or done without charge. ---
examples: Drinks for the band are gratis.
The first consultation is gratis.
Parking was gratis for anyone with a ticket.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb after a verb: They did the work gratis. Formal or humorous; in everyday speech Americans say free.

entries.meaning: Not necessary and without a good reason, often in a way that offends people. ---
examples: Critics complained about the gratuitous violence in the film.
That insult was completely gratuitous.
Each sequel was more gratuitous than the last.
entries.contrast: Not 'grateful' and, in everyday use, not 'free': gratuitous means done for no good reason. It is related to gratuity ('a tip'), but the meanings have split.

entries.meaning: Grave has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The patient is in grave danger.
Leaving the door unlocked was a grave mistake.
Climate change is one of the gravest threats we face.
The doctor came in with a grave expression.
His voice was grave when he called.

senses.head: Very serious and worrying
examples: The patient is in grave danger.
Leaving the door unlocked was a grave mistake.
Climate change is one of the gravest threats we face.

senses.head: Looking or sounding serious and worried
examples: The doctor came in with a grave expression.
His voice was grave when he called.

entries.contrast: Also a noun: a grave — могила.

entries.meaning: Gravelly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He had a deep, gravelly voice from years of smoking.
Her voice gets more gravelly when she's tired.
We drove slowly down the gravelly road.
The riverbank is gravelly and hard to walk on.

senses.head: Of a voice: low and rough
examples: He had a deep, gravelly voice from years of smoking.
Her voice gets more gravelly when she's tired.

senses.head: Covered with or full of small stones
examples: We drove slowly down the gravelly road.
The riverbank is gravelly and hard to walk on.

entries.contrast: An -ly adjective, not an adverb, and spelled with ll: gravel + -ly.

entries.meaning: Relating to gravity. ---
examples: The moon's gravitational pull causes the tides.
Scientists detected gravitational waves for the first time in 2015.
Jupiter's gravitational field is much stronger than Earth's.

entries.meaning: Having gray or white hair. ---
examples: A gray-haired woman opened the door.
My dad was completely gray-haired by forty.
The audience was mostly gray-haired retirees.
entries.contrast: American spelling gray; British grey-haired.

entries.meaning: Slightly gray. ---
examples: The sky was a grayish blue.
His skin looked grayish and he said he felt sick.
The water turned grayish after the storm.
entries.contrast: American spelling grayish; British greyish.

entries.meaning: Covered with a thin layer of oil, fat or grease. ---
examples: Pour the batter into a greased pan.
Make sure the baking sheet is well greased.

examples: I grew up wearing hand-me-down clothes.

Our first car was a hand-me-down minivan from my parents.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: I wore my sister's hand-me-downs.

entries.meaning: Of fighting: at very close range, with the hands or hand weapons. ---
examples: Soldiers are trained in hand-to-hand combat.
The movie ends with a hand-to-hand fight on a rooftop.
It was brutal hand-to-hand fighting in the streets.
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, written without hyphens: They fought hand to hand.

entries.meaning: Having only just enough money to live on, with nothing saved. ---
examples: They lived a hand-to-mouth existence for years.
Many gig workers have a hand-to-mouth lifestyle.
He grew up in a hand-to-mouth family in rural Ohio.
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, written without hyphens: They lived hand to mouth.

entries.meaning: Small enough to hold and use in your hand. ---
examples: The kids played handheld video games in the car.
He shot the whole film with a handheld camera.
The scanner is light and fully handheld.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a handheld is a small device, such as a game console.

entries.meaning: Having a physical or mental disability. ---
examples: Park in the handicapped spaces only if you have a permit.
The bathroom on the first floor is handicapped-accessible.
The program was set up in the 1970s for handicapped children.
entries.contrast: Now considered dated and often offensive about people; say disabled or a person with a disability. It survives on signs and in set phrases: handicapped parking, handicapped-accessible.

entries.meaning: Made by hand, not by machine. ---
examples: She gave me a handmade birthday card.
All their soaps are handmade.
The market is full of handmade pottery.

entries.meaning: Clear and easy, with no doubt at all. ---
examples: She was the hands-down winner.
This movie is the hands-down favorite for best picture.
It was a hands-down victory for the home team.
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, usually without a hyphen: She won hands down; It's hands down the best pizza in town.

entries.meaning: Letting people do things their own way, without getting involved. ---
examples: My boss has a hands-off management style.
The government took a hands-off approach to the industry.
My parents were more hands-off with my younger brother.

entries.meaning: Hands-on has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The museum has lots of hands-on exhibits for kids.
Nothing beats hands-on experience.
The course is very hands-on.
She's a hands-on manager who knows every client.
My dad was more hands-on with us than his father ever was.

senses.head: Involving doing things yourself, not just reading or watching
examples: The museum has lots of hands-on exhibits for kids.
Nothing beats hands-on experience.
The course is very hands-on.

senses.head: Personally involved in the work and its details
examples: She's a hands-on manager who knows every client.
My dad was more hands-on with us than his father ever was.

entries.meaning: Handsome has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Her husband is tall and handsome.
He was the handsomest guy in our class.
What a handsome little boy!
They live in a handsome brick house on Elm Street.
That's a handsome leather jacket.
She sold the company for a handsome profit.
They offered a handsome reward for the lost dog.

senses.head: Good-looking, especially of a man
examples: Her husband is tall and handsome.
He was the handsomest guy in our class.
What a handsome little boy!

senses.head: Of a thing or an animal: attractive and well made
examples: They live in a handsome brick house on Elm Street.
That's a handsome leather jacket.

senses.head: Of money: large in amount
examples: She sold the company for a handsome profit.
They offered a handsome reward for the lost dog.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — handsomer, handsomest; more handsome
entries.contrast: About a man, handsome is the usual word for good-looking; pretty and beautiful are mostly for women. About a woman, handsome means striking and strong-featured, not delicate. The d is silent.

entries.meaning: Written by hand with a pen or pencil. ---
examples: She left a handwritten note on the door.
The recipe is handwritten on an old index card.
A handwritten thank-you letter means a lot.

entries.meaning: Handy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: This app is really handy for splitting the bill.
Keep the receipt — it might come in handy.
The new version is even handier than the old one.
Do you have a pen handy?
Keep a flashlight handy in case the power goes out.
My husband is handy with tools.
It helps to be handy if you buy an old house.

senses.head: Useful and easy to use
examples: This app is really handy for splitting the bill.
Keep the receipt — it might come in handy.
The new version is even handier than the old one.

senses.head: Near and easy to reach
examples: Do you have a pen handy?
Keep a flashlight handy in case the power goes out.

senses.head: Good at fixing or making things with your hands
examples: My husband is handy with tools.
It helps to be handy if you buy an old house.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only after a verb or a noun
entries.contrast: Come in handy means turn out to be useful: This flashlight will come in handy.

entries.meaning: Done without any plan or order. ---
examples: Books were stacked in a haphazard way on the floor.
Their approach to safety was pretty haphazard.
The second half of the project was even more haphazard than the first.

entries.meaning: Unlucky, often in a way that looks a little foolish. ---
examples: The hapless tourists got lost again.
The team's hapless defense gave up six goals.
The hapless intern spilled coffee on the CEO.

entries.meaning: Cheerful and not worried about the future. ---
examples: He was a happy-go-lucky kid who made friends everywhere.
She seems happy-go-lucky, but she works incredibly hard.
My younger brother was always more happy-go-lucky than me.

entries.meaning: Tired, anxious and stressed because of too many problems or demands. ---
examples: A harassed mom was trying to calm three kids at the checkout.
The waiter looked harassed and overworked.
By Friday, the staff looked more harassed than ever.
entries.contrast: The adjective describes someone stressed by too many demands (a harassed waiter). She was harassed at work is the passive verb: someone treated her in a hostile or sexual way, a much more serious meaning. Some Americans stress the first syllable: HAIR-uhst.

entries.meaning: Not having enough money, or not enough of something you need. ---
examples: We were pretty hard up when I was a kid.
The school is hard up for volunteers this year.
After the plant closed, the town was more hard up than ever.
entries.position: predicative only — never before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — more hard up, most hard up

entries.meaning: Fixed and not able to be changed. ---
examples: There are no hard-and-fast rules for raising kids.
We don't have a hard-and-fast deadline yet.
It's more of a guideline than a hard-and-fast rule.
entries.contrast: Usually in the negative: There are no hard-and-fast rules.

entries.meaning: Tough and not easily shocked, because of hard experience. ---
examples: The story is told by a hard-bitten detective.
Even hard-bitten reporters were shocked by the photos.
The old sailors were more hard-bitten than anyone else on the crew.

entries.meaning: Hard-boiled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I packed two hard-boiled eggs for lunch.
Do you want your eggs hard-boiled or soft?
He loves old hard-boiled detective novels.
She plays a hard-boiled cop in the new series.

senses.head: Of an egg: boiled until the yolk is solid
examples: I packed two hard-boiled eggs for lunch.
Do you want your eggs hard-boiled or soft?

senses.head: Tough and unemotional, especially in crime fiction
examples: He loves old hard-boiled detective novels.
She plays a hard-boiled cop in the new series.

entries.comparison: not gradable — sense 2 can take more: more hard-boiled

entries.meaning: Won or achieved only with great effort against strong opposition. ---
examples: It was a hard-fought victory over a tough team.
Workers won hard-fought gains in the new contract.
The game was close and hard-fought from start to finish.

entries.meaning: Hard-hitting has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The newspaper published a hard-hitting report on police misconduct.
Her documentary is hard-hitting and honest.
This year's anti-smoking ads are more hard-hitting than last year's.
He's a big, hard-hitting linebacker.
It was a hard-hitting game with lots of injuries.

senses.head: Direct and forceful in dealing with a serious problem
examples: The newspaper published a hard-hitting report on police misconduct.
Her documentary is hard-hitting and honest.
This year's anti-smoking ads are more hard-hitting than last year's.

senses.head: In sports: hitting or tackling with a lot of force
examples: He's a big, hard-hitting linebacker.
It was a hard-hitting game with lots of injuries.

entries.meaning: Refusing to change your views or compromise, especially in politics. ---
examples: The governor took a hard-line position on crime.
Hard-line members of the party blocked the deal.
His views have become more hard-line over the years.
entries.contrast: Also written hardline. A person with these views is a hard-liner.

entries.meaning: Tough, practical and not influenced by feelings. ---
examples: She's a hard-nosed negotiator.
He takes a hard-nosed approach to business.
The new coach is more hard-nosed than the last one.

entries.meaning: Not able to hear well, but not completely deaf. ---
examples: The theater offers headsets for hard-of-hearing guests.
My grandpa is a little hard of hearing, so speak up.
The school has services for deaf and hard-of-hearing students.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (hard-of-hearing students); after a verb it is usually three separate words: My grandpa is hard of hearing. Deaf means unable to hear at all.

entries.meaning: Hard-pressed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal.
I'm hard-pressed to remember the last time it snowed here.
Hard-pressed families are struggling with rising rents.
Hospitals were more hard-pressed than ever that winter.
The hard-pressed staff worked double shifts.

senses.head: Having great difficulty doing something
examples: You'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal.
I'm hard-pressed to remember the last time it snowed here.

senses.head: Under a lot of pressure, especially from lack of money or time
examples: Hard-pressed families are struggling with rising rents.
Hospitals were more hard-pressed than ever that winter.
The hard-pressed staff worked double shifts.

entries.position: both — sense 1 only after a verb

entries.meaning: Hardcore has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only the hardcore fans stayed in the rain.
She's a hardcore gamer.
My brother is way more hardcore about fitness than I am.
That was a hardcore workout.
Camping in January is pretty hardcore.

senses.head: Very committed and enthusiastic, more than most people
examples: Only the hardcore fans stayed in the rain.
She's a hardcore gamer.
My brother is way more hardcore about fitness than I am.

senses.head: Extreme or very intense
examples: That was a hardcore workout.
Camping in January is pretty hardcore.

entries.contrast: Also written hard-core. In hardcore pornography it means sexually explicit; hardcore punk is a style of music.

entries.meaning: Of a book: with a stiff, strong cover. ---
examples: The hardcover edition costs thirty dollars.
I bought a hardcover copy for my dad.
The library replaced its worn hardcover books with paperbacks.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: The book came out in hardcover. British English prefers hardback.

entries.meaning: Hardened has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a hardened criminal with a long record.
After years at war, she had become hardened to violence.
He came back from prison more hardened than before.
The blade is made of hardened steel.
Scrape off the hardened glue before you paint.

senses.head: Made tough by experience, so no longer shocked or upset
examples: He's a hardened criminal with a long record.
After years at war, she had become hardened to violence.
He came back from prison more hardened than before.

senses.head: Made physically hard or firm
examples: The blade is made of hardened steel.
Scrape off the hardened glue before you paint.

entries.meaning: Hardheaded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We need to take a hardheaded look at the budget.
She's a hardheaded businesswoman.
My dad is too hardheaded to ask for directions.
Why are you being so hardheaded?
He's even more hardheaded than his mother.

senses.head: Practical and realistic, not emotional
examples: We need to take a hardheaded look at the budget.
She's a hardheaded businesswoman.

senses.head: Stubborn and unwilling to listen
examples: My dad is too hardheaded to ask for directions.
Why are you being so hardheaded?
He's even more hardheaded than his mother.

entries.meaning: Strict and unwilling to compromise, especially in politics. ---
examples: The party's hardline wing opposed any compromise.
Critics say the new policy is too hardline.
The talks collapsed after both sides grew more hardline.
entries.contrast: Also written hard-line; the meaning is the same.

entries.meaning: Poor, and needing very hard work to make a living. ---
examples: He grew up on a hardscrabble farm in West Texas.
Her memoir describes a hardscrabble childhood in Appalachia.
It was a hardscrabble mining town with one diner and two bars.
entries.form: compound — hard + scrabble, to scratch around for something

entries.meaning: Hardy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only a few hardy hikers made it to the top.
Goats are hardy animals.
The hardiest fans showed up in the snow.
These roses are hardy enough for Minnesota winters.
Kale is hardier than lettuce.

senses.head: Strong and able to live through difficult conditions
examples: Only a few hardy hikers made it to the top.
Goats are hardy animals.
The hardiest fans showed up in the snow.

senses.head: Of a plant: able to survive cold weather outdoors
examples: These roses are hardy enough for Minnesota winters.
Kale is hardier than lettuce.

entries.contrast: Do not confuse with hearty (warm and friendly; large, as in a hearty meal), which sounds similar.

entries.meaning: Foolish and not likely to work. ---
examples: He's always coming up with harebrained schemes.
That idea is completely harebrained.
Her latest plan is even more harebrained than the last.
entries.form: compound — hare + brain + -ed: with a brain like a rabbit's
entries.contrast: Spelled with hare (a kind of rabbit), not hair.

entries.meaning: Causing damage or injury. ---
examples: Too much sun is harmful to your skin.
The factory released harmful chemicals into the river.
Some doctors think sugar is more harmful than fat.

entries.meaning: Harmless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Most spiders are harmless to people.
The substance is completely harmless.
Garter snakes look scary, but they're harmless.
It was just harmless fun.
He's a little annoying, but harmless.

senses.head: Not able to cause damage or injury
examples: Most spiders are harmless to people.
The substance is completely harmless.
Garter snakes look scary, but they're harmless.

senses.head: Not meant to hurt or offend anyone
examples: It was just harmless fun.
He's a little annoying, but harmless.

entries.meaning: Harmonious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They have a harmonious relationship with their neighbors.
The office has become much more harmonious since the reorganization.
Life at home was not always harmonious.
The room has a harmonious mix of colors.
The choir's voices were beautifully harmonious.

senses.head: Friendly and peaceful, without disagreement
examples: They have a harmonious relationship with their neighbors.
The office has become much more harmonious since the reorganization.
Life at home was not always harmonious.

senses.head: Of colors, sounds or parts: fitting together in a pleasant way
examples: The room has a harmonious mix of colors.
The choir's voices were beautifully harmonious.

entries.meaning: Stressed and rushed because of too many demands. ---
examples: A harried waitress finally took our order.
Parents look harried during the holiday rush.
The nurses were more harried than usual on Monday.
entries.contrast: Close to harassed in its adjective sense, and more common in American English. Nothing to do with the name Harry.

entries.meaning: Extremely frightening or upsetting to live through. ---
examples: The survivors described a harrowing night in the lifeboat.
The documentary is harrowing but important.
It was the most harrowing experience of my life.

entries.meaning: Harsh has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The judge handed down a harsh sentence.
Don't be so harsh on yourself.
Her harshest critics were her own teammates.
These plants survive harsh desert conditions.
Winters in North Dakota are harsh.
The climate was harsher than they had expected.
The harsh office lights gave me a headache.
This soap is too harsh for a baby's skin.

senses.head: Unkind, cruel or too severe
examples: The judge handed down a harsh sentence.
Don't be so harsh on yourself.
Her harshest critics were her own teammates.

senses.head: Of conditions or weather: very difficult to live in
examples: These plants survive harsh desert conditions.
Winters in North Dakota are harsh.
The climate was harsher than they had expected.

senses.head: Too strong or unpleasant for the eyes, ears or skin
examples: The harsh office lights gave me a headache.
This soap is too harsh for a baby's skin.

entries.meaning: Belonging to a strictly Orthodox Jewish movement. ---
examples: Brooklyn has a large Hasidic community.
Their neighbors are Hasidic.
Hasidic men often wear black coats and hats.
entries.contrast: Always a capital H. Also spelled Chasidic, and some speakers begin it with the throaty sound of German Bach.

entries.meaning: Hasty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Let's not make any hasty decisions.
Maybe I was too hasty in judging him.
Looking back, the decision seems hasty.
We ate a hasty breakfast and ran for the bus.
The robbers made a hasty exit.
The second draft was even hastier than the first.

senses.head: Done too quickly, without enough thought
examples: Let's not make any hasty decisions.
Maybe I was too hasty in judging him.
Looking back, the decision seems hasty.

senses.head: Done or made very quickly because there is little time
examples: We ate a hasty breakfast and ran for the bus.
The robbers made a hasty exit.
The second draft was even hastier than the first.

entries.meaning: Strongly disliked by many people. ---
examples: He was the most hated man in town.
The new parking rules are widely hated.
Traffic cameras are a hated part of city life.
entries.contrast: Not hateful: a hated person is hated by others; a hateful person is full of hate.

entries.meaning: Full of hate, or very cruel toward others. ---
examples: He posted hateful comments online.
What a hateful thing to say!
Her words were more hateful than anything I'd heard before.
entries.contrast: Hateful usually means full of hate (hateful comments), not hated by others.

entries.meaning: Behaving as if you are better than other people. ---
examples: The haughty waiter ignored our table.
She gave me a cold, haughty look.
He's become even haughtier since his promotion.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — haughtier, haughtiest; more haughty

entries.meaning: Haunted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Kids say the old house on the hill is haunted.
We went through a haunted house at Halloween.
It's supposedly the most haunted hotel in America.
He had a haunted look in his eyes.
She is still haunted by the accident.

senses.head: Believed to be visited by ghosts
examples: Kids say the old house on the hill is haunted.
We went through a haunted house at Halloween.
It's supposedly the most haunted hotel in America.

senses.head: Troubled for a long time by a memory or a worry
examples: He had a haunted look in his eyes.
She is still haunted by the accident.

entries.meaning: Beautiful, sad or frightening in a way that stays in your mind. ---
examples: The song has a haunting melody.
Her photographs of the war are haunting.
It's one of the most haunting movies I've ever seen.
entries.contrast: Not haunted: a haunting song stays in your mind; a haunted house has ghosts.

entries.meaning: Of or from Hawaii, its people, language or culture. ---
examples: He wore a Hawaiian shirt to the barbecue.
Hawaiian pizza has ham and pineapple on it.
She's taking a class in the Hawaiian language.
entries.contrast: Always a capital H. As a noun, a Hawaiian strictly means a Native Hawaiian; someone who simply lives there is a Hawaii resident.

entries.meaning: Able to notice small details; watching very closely. ---
examples: A hawk-eyed fan spotted the mistake in the credits.
The teacher is hawk-eyed during exams.
Our editor is even more hawk-eyed than the proofreader.

entries.meaning: Hawkish has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The senator is known for his hawkish views on foreign policy.
His advisers were more hawkish than the public.
The Fed's hawkish tone worried investors.
Stocks fell after hawkish comments from the central bank.

senses.head: Favoring military force or tough action in foreign policy
examples: The senator is known for his hawkish views on foreign policy.
His advisers were more hawkish than the public.

senses.head: In economics: favoring higher interest rates to fight inflation
examples: The Fed's hawkish tone worried investors.
Stocks fell after hawkish comments from the central bank.

entries.form: -ish from hawk, a supporter of force

entries.meaning: Not working properly, or out of control. ---
examples: My phone went haywire after the update.
The thermostat has gone haywire again.
Everything went haywire when the power came back on.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always after go: go haywire
entries.form: hay + wire: the wire used to tie hay bales, which tangled easily

entries.meaning: Dangerous, especially to health or safety. ---
examples: The plant disposes of hazardous waste.
Smoking is hazardous to your health.
Driving is more hazardous in winter.

entries.meaning: Light brown with some green or gold, especially of eyes. ---
examples: She has big hazel eyes.
His eyes are hazel, not green.
The baby's eyes turned hazel by her first birthday.
entries.contrast: Mostly about eyes: a light brown mixed with green or gold, lighter than a typical Russian карий. Plain dark brown eyes are just brown. As a noun, hazel is also the tree that gives hazelnuts.

entries.meaning: Hazy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a hot, hazy afternoon.
The mountains looked hazy in the distance.
The sky is hazier than usual because of the wildfires.
My memory of that night is a little hazy.
I'm still hazy on the details of the plan.

senses.head: Of air or sky: not clear because of mist, smoke or dust
examples: It was a hot, hazy afternoon.
The mountains looked hazy in the distance.
The sky is hazier than usual because of the wildfires.

senses.head: Not clear in your mind; vague
examples: My memory of that night is a little hazy.
I'm still hazy on the details of the plan.

entries.meaning: Head-on has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Two people were hurt in a head-on collision on Route 9.
It was a head-on crash at highway speed.
The mayor took a head-on approach to the housing crisis.
The two sides are headed for a head-on clash over taxes.

senses.head: With the fronts of two things hitting each other
examples: Two people were hurt in a head-on collision on Route 9.
It was a head-on crash at highway speed.

senses.head: Direct, without avoiding a problem or a conflict
examples: The mayor took a head-on approach to the housing crisis.
The two sides are headed for a head-on clash over taxes.

entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb: The cars collided head-on; We need to face the problem head-on.

entries.meaning: Involving direct competition between two people or teams. ---
examples: The two candidates will meet in a head-to-head debate.
It's a head-to-head battle for first place.
In head-to-head matchups, Boston has won six of the last ten.
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, often without hyphens: The two stores compete head to head.

entries.meaning: Without a head. ---
examples: The story is about a headless horseman.
We found a headless doll in the attic.
The statue has stood headless since the earthquake.

entries.meaning: Headlong has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He made a headlong dive into the pool.
She took a headlong fall down the stairs.
The headlong rush into new technology worries some teachers.
It was a headlong flight from the burning building.

senses.head: With the head first
examples: He made a headlong dive into the pool.
She took a headlong fall down the stairs.

senses.head: Very fast and without careful thought
examples: The headlong rush into new technology worries some teachers.
It was a headlong flight from the burning building.

entries.contrast: More often an adverb: She rushed headlong into marriage; He fell headlong down the stairs.

entries.meaning: Determined to do things your own way, without listening to advice. ---
examples: She was a headstrong teenager.
He's too headstrong to take anyone's advice.
Their second child is even more headstrong than the first.

entries.meaning: Heady has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Those were the heady days of the dot-com boom.
Winning the title was a heady experience for such a young team.
It was the headiest moment of her career.
It's a heady red wine.
The heady scent of jasmine filled the garden.

senses.head: So exciting that it makes you feel a little out of control
examples: Those were the heady days of the dot-com boom.
Winning the title was a heady experience for such a young team.
It was the headiest moment of her career.

senses.head: Of a drink or a smell: strong, making you feel a little drunk or dizzy
examples: It's a heady red wine.
The heady scent of jasmine filled the garden.

entries.meaning: Making a wound, an illness or a hurt feeling better. ---
examples: Time has a healing effect on grief.
She rubbed a healing salve into the cut.
The weekend at the lake was healing in a way none of us expected.

entries.meaning: Careful about eating well and staying fit. ---
examples: Health-conscious shoppers read every label.
My roommate has gotten very health-conscious since January.
The menu was redesigned for a more health-conscious crowd.

entries.meaning: Unable to hear well. ---
examples: The theater has headsets for hearing-impaired guests.
Her younger son is hearing-impaired.
Hearing-impaired students sit near the front.
entries.contrast: Many deaf people prefer deaf or hard of hearing to this term.

entries.meaning: Good for the heart, of a food or a diet. ---
examples: Olive oil is a heart-healthy fat.
The cafeteria marks its heart-healthy entrees with a green dot.
Salmon is more heart-healthy than steak.

entries.meaning: Shaped like a valentine heart. ---
examples: He gave her a heart-shaped locket.
The cookies came out lopsided rather than heart-shaped.
A heart-shaped leaf floated in the puddle.

entries.meaning: So exciting or frightening that it seems to stop your heart. ---
examples: The last lap was heart-stopping.
It was a heart-stopping moment when the lights went out.
Nothing is more heart-stopping than a phone call at 3 a.m.

entries.meaning: Honest and personal, of a conversation. ---
examples: We finally had a heart-to-heart talk about money.
A heart-to-heart conversation with his dad changed his mind.
She scheduled a heart-to-heart chat with each of her students.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: we had a heart-to-heart means the talk itself.

entries.meaning: Causing deep sadness. ---
examples: The documentary was heartbreaking.
She told a heartbreaking story about the fire.
Losing by one point was the most heartbreaking part.
entries.contrast: Heartbreaking describes the thing, heartbroken the person: a heartbreaking story left her heartbroken.

entries.meaning: Feeling deep sadness, especially over a loss. ---
examples: She was heartbroken when the dog died.
He came home heartbroken after the audition.
A heartbroken fan stood outside the stadium all night.

entries.meaning: Making you feel more hopeful. ---
examples: The turnout was heartening.
It is heartening to see so many volunteers.
We got a heartening update from the hospital.

entries.meaning: Sincere and deeply meant. ---
examples: She sent a heartfelt apology.
His thanks were clearly heartfelt.
The eulogy was simple and heartfelt.

entries.meaning: Cruel, with no pity for other people. ---
examples: It was heartless to fire her by text.
Don't be so heartless.
He is the most heartless landlord I have ever had.

entries.meaning: Causing sharp pity or grief. ---
examples: The photographs from the flood were heartrending.
She let out a heartrending cry.
It is heartrending to watch them say goodbye.

entries.meaning: Very unhappy, especially over love or loss. ---
examples: He was heartsick over the breakup for months.
She came back from the visit heartsick.
A heartsick letter arrived a week later.

entries.meaning: Giving a warm, happy feeling. ---
examples: The reunion video is heartwarming.
It was a heartwarming gesture.
Nothing is more heartwarming than seeing the two of them together again.

entries.meaning: Hearty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We had a hearty breakfast before the hike.
He has a hearty appetite for someone so small.
The stew is heartier than the soup.
She gave us a hearty welcome.
A hearty laugh came from the kitchen.

senses.head: Large and filling, of food or of an appetite
examples: We had a hearty breakfast before the hike.
He has a hearty appetite for someone so small.
The stew is heartier than the soup.

senses.head: Warm, loud and full of feeling
examples: She gave us a hearty welcome.
A hearty laugh came from the kitchen.

entries.meaning: Able to take high heat without damage. ---
examples: Use a heat-resistant bowl for the chocolate.

entries.form: -ed from humiliate — how the person feels
entries.contrast: humiliated is how you feel; humiliating is what makes you feel that way: a humiliating defeat, a humiliated team.

entries.meaning: Making you feel ashamed and foolish. ---
examples: The team suffered a humiliating defeat.
Having to ask my parents for money was humiliating.
It was the most humiliating day of my life.
entries.form: -ing from humiliate — what causes the feeling

entries.meaning: Informal: extremely big. ---
examples: They live in a humongous house on the lake.
The portions at that diner are humongous.
He ordered a humongous plate of nachos.
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely humongous, not very humongous
entries.contrast: Informal and a little playful; use huge or enormous in formal writing.

entries.meaning: Having no sense of humor; too serious. ---
examples: The new manager is strict and humorless.
She gave a humorless laugh.
He's the most humorless person I've ever worked with.
entries.contrast: American spelling is humorless; British English writes humourless.

entries.meaning: Funny and entertaining. ---
examples: He gave a humorous speech at the wedding.
Her column is smart and humorous.
The second half of the book is more humorous than the first.
entries.contrast: Spelled humorous in both American and British English, even though British humour has a u.

entries.meaning: With the back and shoulders bent forward. ---
examples: He sat hunched over his laptop all day.
She walked with hunched shoulders against the cold.
An old man sat hunched on the bench.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Hungary, its people or its language. ---
examples: She makes a great Hungarian goulash.
My grandparents were Hungarian.
Hungarian grammar is famously difficult.
entries.contrast: Always a capital letter. a Hungarian is a person and Hungarian is the language — both nouns.

entries.meaning: Informal: fine, with no problems. ---
examples: Everything is hunky-dory at home.
He acts like everything's hunky-dory, but he's worried.
The deal looked hunky-dory until the lawyers read it.
entries.contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned; often used ironically: Everything's not exactly hunky-dory.

entries.meaning: Hunted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He had a hunted look in his eyes.
After weeks on the run, she looked thin and hunted.
After the escape he was a hunted man.
Wolves were once the most hunted animals in the state.

senses.head: Looking frightened and worried, as if someone is chasing you
examples: He had a hunted look in his eyes.
After weeks on the run, she looked thin and hunted.

senses.head: Being searched for or chased in order to be caught or killed
examples: After the escape he was a hunted man.
Wolves were once the most hunted animals in the state.

entries.meaning: Done quickly because there is not much time. ---
examples: We ate a hurried breakfast and ran for the bus.
His goodbye was short and hurried.
The second draft felt more hurried than the first.

entries.meaning: Hurt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Are you hurt? Can you stand up?
Two players were badly hurt in the collision.
The hurt hiker was carried down the trail.
She was hurt that nobody remembered her birthday.
I tried not to show my hurt feelings.
He was more hurt by her silence than by her words.

senses.head: Injured, with pain in part of the body
examples: Are you hurt? Can you stand up?
Two players were badly hurt in the collision.
The hurt hiker was carried down the trail.

senses.head: Upset and offended by what someone said or did
examples: She was hurt that nobody remembered her birthday.
I tried not to show my hurt feelings.
He was more hurt by her silence than by her words.

entries.form: past participle of hurt — the same form as the verb
entries.contrast: The past participle is hurt, never hurted. For a serious wound, injured or wounded is more exact.

entries.meaning: Making someone feel upset or offended. ---
examples: That was a really hurtful thing to say.
His comments about her weight were hurtful.
Being ignored was more hurtful than being criticized.

entries.meaning: Informal: kept secret. ---
examples: The project is all very hush-hush.
They held a hush-hush meeting with the investors.
The wedding plans were even more hush-hush than the engagement.

entries.meaning: Very quiet, or spoken quietly. ---
examples: They spoke in hushed voices so they wouldn't wake the baby.
The courtroom was hushed as the verdict was read.
A hushed crowd watched the final putt.

entries.meaning: Husky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has a warm, husky voice.
His voice was husky from shouting at the game.
Her voice got huskier as the night went on.
A husky young farmhand lifted the bales.
He was a husky kid who grew into a football player.

senses.head: Of a voice: low and slightly rough
examples: She has a warm, husky voice.
His voice was husky from shouting at the game.
Her voice got huskier as the night went on.

senses.head: Of a person: big, strong and heavy
examples: A husky young farmhand lifted the bales.
He was a husky kid who grew into a football player.

entries.contrast: a husky is also a noun — a sled dog. In US stores, husky sizes are clothes for heavier boys.

entries.meaning: Made by combining two different kinds of things. ---
examples: We bought a hybrid car to save on gas.
The company switched to a hybrid work model — three days in the office, two at home.
The tomato plants in the garden are hybrid.
entries.contrast: a hybrid is also a noun: She drives a hybrid.

entries.meaning: Having enough water in the body or skin. ---
examples: Drink plenty of water to stay hydrated in the heat.
This lotion keeps your skin hydrated.
I feel more hydrated since I started carrying a water bottle.

entries.meaning: Moved or operated by the pressure of water or oil. ---
examples: The truck has a hydraulic lift.
The mechanic found a leak in the hydraulic brakes.
Hydraulic fracturing is used to get oil and gas out of rock.

entries.meaning: Producing electricity from the force of moving water. ---
examples: Hoover Dam is a huge hydroelectric plant.
The state gets most of its power from hydroelectric dams.
Hydroelectric energy is cheap in the Pacific Northwest.

entries.meaning: Growing plants in water with nutrients, without soil. ---
examples: They grow lettuce in a hydroponic greenhouse.
The restaurant has its own hydroponic herb garden.
Hydroponic farms use much less water than ordinary fields.

entries.meaning: Clean and not likely to spread disease. ---
examples: The kitchen didn't look very hygienic.
Nurses wear gloves for hygienic reasons.
Paper towels are more hygienic than hand dryers.

entries.meaning: Too active, and unable to stay still or focus. ---
examples: Sugar makes my kids hyperactive.
He was diagnosed as a hyperactive child.
The puppy is even more hyperactive after a nap.

entries.meaning: Hyperbolic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Calling it 'the worst day in history' is a little hyperbolic.
The ad made hyperbolic claims about the product.
The headlines got more hyperbolic every day.
We studied hyperbolic functions in calculus.
The comet followed a hyperbolic path.

senses.head: Exaggerated; saying something is much bigger or worse than it is
examples: Calling it 'the worst day in history' is a little hyperbolic.
The ad made hyperbolic claims about the product.
The headlines got more hyperbolic every day.

senses.head: In math: relating to a hyperbola
examples: We studied hyperbolic functions in calculus.
The comet followed a hyperbolic path.

entries.comparison: more/most — more hyperbolic, most hyperbolic (in the 'exaggerated' sense)

entries.meaning: Too easily affected, upset or offended. ---
examples: Some people are hypersensitive to noise.
He's hypersensitive about his height.
Her skin became even more hypersensitive after the treatment.

entries.meaning: Hypnotic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The song has a slow, hypnotic beat.
Watching the waves was almost hypnotic.
Her voice was even more hypnotic in person.
The patient was put into a hypnotic trance.
Some therapists use hypnotic techniques to treat anxiety.

senses.head: Holding your attention in a way that makes you feel calm or sleepy
examples: The song has a slow, hypnotic beat.
Watching the waves was almost hypnotic.
Her voice was even more hypnotic in person.

senses.head: Relating to hypnosis
examples: The patient was put into a hypnotic trance.
Some therapists use hypnotic techniques to treat anxiety.

entries.meaning: Hypnotized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids sat hypnotized by the cartoon.
I was hypnotized by the northern lights.
The hypnotized volunteer started clucking like a chicken.
She claims she quit smoking after being hypnotized.

senses.head: So interested in something that you cannot look away
examples: The kids sat hypnotized by the cartoon.
I was hypnotized by the northern lights.

senses.head: Put into a state of hypnosis
examples: The hypnotized volunteer started clucking like a chicken.
She claims she quit smoking after being hypnotized.

entries.contrast: American spelling is hypnotized; British English also writes hypnotised.

entries.meaning: Saying you believe one thing but doing the opposite. ---
examples: It's hypocritical of him to lecture us about saving money.
Voters were angry at the hypocritical senator.
Nothing is more hypocritical than preaching honesty and then lying.
entries.takes: of + person + to-infinitive: It's hypocritical of him to complain

entries.meaning: Used to inject drugs under the skin. ---
examples: The nurse filled a hypodermic syringe.
Kids found a used hypodermic needle in the park.
The vaccine was given by hypodermic injection.

entries.meaning: Imagined as possible, but not real or not yet true. ---
examples: Let me ask you a hypothetical question.
The danger is not just hypothetical — it has happened before.
The lawyers argued about a hypothetical situation.

entries.meaning: Hysterical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The mother became hysterical when she couldn't find her son.
Stop being hysterical and listen to me.
The crowd grew more hysterical as the fire spread.
Her impression of the boss was hysterical.
It's the most hysterical movie I've seen all year.

senses.head: Out of control because of strong emotion, such as fear or grief
examples: The mother became hysterical when she couldn't find her son.
Stop being hysterical and listen to me.
The crowd grew more hysterical as the fire spread.

senses.head: Informal: extremely funny
examples: Her impression of the boss was hysterical.
It's the most hysterical movie I've seen all year.

entries.contrast: In informal American English hysterical very often means very funny: That video is hysterical!
